title: Criteria for Feasible Monte Carlo Stochastic Simulations of Bosonic Markovian Open Quantum Dynamics
authors: Toma Yoneya, Kazuya Fujimoto, Yuki Kawaguchi
abstract: The Monte Carlo sampling of the stochastic differential equations (SDEs) based on the quasiprobability distribution function, such as the Glauber--Sudarshan P, Wigner, and Husimi Q functions provides a powerful framework for investigating bosonic open quantum many-body dynamics described by the Gorini--Kossakowski--Sudarshan--Lindblad (GKSL) equation, while considering the effects of quantum fluctuations beyond the mean-field approximation. However, the stochastic Monte Carlo simulation is possible only when the corresponding Fokker--Planck equation has a positive-semidefinite diffusion matrix, and the general conditions for the diffusion matrix to be positive semidefinite have remained unclear. In this work, starting from the path integral formulation, we first derive the sufficient conditions under which the diffusion matrix is positive semidefinite for an arbitrary Hamiltonian, jump operators, and choice of quasiprobability distribution functions. We also analytically derive the corresponding SDEs to be solved. We then investigate the dynamics of the GKSL equation in the thermodynamic limit and show that, depending on the form of the jump operators, the mean-field approximation may fail to describe the dynamics accurately, making stochastic Monte Carlo simulations indispensable. Furthermore, we derive the sufficient conditions under which the higher-order quantum fluctuation terms beyond the Fokker--Planck description vanish identically, even when the jump operators contain quadratic terms. Under these conditions, whenever the corresponding SDEs can be derived, the stochastic Monte Carlo simulation reproduces the exact dynamics. These results clarify the conditions under which the stochastic Monte Carlo simulations are both feasible and necessary for accurately describing the dynamics governed by the GKSL equation in phase space.
summary: This paper develops rigorous mathematical criteria to determine when stochastic Monte Carlo simulations can accurately model bosonic open quantum dynamics governed by the GKSL equation. By analyzing the positive semidefiniteness of the diffusion matrix derived from path integrals, the authors clarify the necessary conditions for these powerful simulation techniques to be both feasible and indispensable over mean-field approximations.
main_problem: The primary goal is establishing rigorous criteria for when Monte Carlo stochastic simulations are mathematically feasible and physically necessary for accurately modeling bosonic open quantum dynamics.
main_result: The authors derive sufficient conditions, starting from the path integral formulation, that guarantee the positive semidefiniteness of the diffusion matrix, thus validating the use of stochastic methods over mean-field approximations.
method: The work combines path integral formulations with phase-space mapping using quasiprobability distributions (P, Wigner, Q functions) to derive and analyze corresponding Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs).
model_or_system: The system involves bosonic open quantum many-body dynamics governed by the Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) equation. The analysis is performed in phase space, considering interactions and dissipation from an environment.
key_observables: Positive semidefiniteness of the diffusion matrix ($\mathbf{A} \succeq 0$), time evolution of quasiprobability functions ($W_s$), and quantum fluctuation terms.
important_parameters: The analysis focuses on the thermodynamic limit, high-occupancy limits, and the nature of the jump operators (e.g., quadratic vs. general).
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on mapping the GKSL equation to a Fokker–Planck type description, which is only valid under specific conditions regarding higher-order quantum fluctuations.
paper_structure: The paper systematically moves from defining the problem (GKSL dynamics) to establishing the mathematical framework (phase-space mapping and path integrals), deriving necessary feasibility criteria for stochastic simulation, and finally analyzing specific limits where approximations break down.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial theoretical guidelines for computational physicists attempting to simulate complex open quantum systems, clarifying when simple mean-field or truncated Wigner approaches are insufficient.
